title: Dynamic memory: new, delete and heap arrays
overview: Module 2 practises basic C++ on judge problems and then introduces the heap. You learn why a local variable dies with its function, how `new` keeps memory alive, how to return an array from a function, and how to "resize" an array by copying.

concepts.explain: Local variables live in the function's stack frame and disappear when it returns.
`new` reserves memory that stays until you `delete` it.
`new int[n]` gives an array on the heap; free it with `delete[]`.
A pointer to memory that has already been freed; reading it is undefined behaviour.
Return a pointer to a heap array, never the address of a local array.
Make a bigger array, copy old items, add new ones, delete the old one.

files.title: Simple Calculator
files.what: Reads two numbers and prints their sum, product and difference in an exact text format.
steps: Read `x` and `y`.
Print `x + y = ...`, `x * y = ...`, `x - y = ...`, each on its own line.
Spaces around the signs must match the judge exactly.
files.watch_out: `x * y` can reach 10^10, which overflows `int`. Declare `long long x, y;`.

check.q: With X, Y up to 10^5, can `x * y` overflow an `int`?
check.a: Yes, 10^10 is bigger than about 2.1*10^9; use `long long` to be safe.

files.title: Capital or Small or Digit

problem.name: Codeforces group - M. Capital or Small or Digit

files.what: Uses ASCII ranges to decide whether a character is a digit, a capital letter or a small letter.
steps: Read `char x`.
If `'0' <= x <= '9'` print `IS DIGIT`, otherwise print `ALPHA`.
Then if `'A' <= x <= 'Z'` print `IS CAPITAL`, else if lowercase print `IS SMALL`.

check.a: Characters are ASCII numbers, and the letters a-z are consecutive codes (97-122).

files.title: Max and Min of three numbers

problem.name: Codeforces group - K. Max and Min

files.what: Finds the smallest and largest of three numbers by starting with `a` and updating.
steps: Set `min = a`, then replace it if `b` or `c` is smaller.
Set `max = a`, then replace it if `b` or `c` is larger.
Print `min max`.

check.q: How would you write this with the built-ins?

files.title: Max of N numbers
files.what: Reads N numbers into an array and scans once, keeping the largest seen so far.
steps: Read `n` and the array `arr`.
Start with `max = arr[0]`.
For every later element, if it is bigger, update `max`.
Print `max`.
files.input_note: First line N, then N numbers.

check.a: If all numbers were negative, 0 would be wrong; the first element is always a valid candidate.

files.title: Reversing an array
files.what: Prints the array from the last index down to 0.
steps: Read `n` and the array.
Loop `i` from `n-1` down to `0`.
Print `arr[i]` followed by a space.
files.input_note: First line N, then N numbers.

check.q: How would you reverse the array in place with `swap`?

files.title: A dynamic variable with new
files.what: Creates an `int` on the heap with `new int` and uses it through the pointer `p`.
steps: `int x = 10;` lives on the stack.
`int *p = new int;` asks the heap for space for one int and returns its address.
`*p = 100;` writes into that space; `cout << *p` prints it.
files.output_note: Prints `100`, the value stored on the heap.
files.watch_out: The program never calls `delete p;` (a small leak), and has a harmless duplicate `return 0;`.

check.q: What should be called when the heap int is no longer needed?

files.title: Static array vs dynamic array
files.what: Fills and prints a normal (stack) array and then a heap array made with `new int[5]`; both use the same `[]` syntax.
steps: `int a[5];` is a fixed stack array; read 5 values and print them.
`int *p = new int[5];` makes a 5-int array on the heap.
`p[i]` works exactly like `a[i]`.
`delete[] p;` gives the heap memory back.
files.input_note: Two lines of 5 integers: one for each array.
files.output_note: Line 1 `1 2 3 4 5` from the static array, line 2 `10 20 30 40 50` from the dynamic one.

files.title: Dangling pointer to a stack variable
files.what: A global pointer is set to the address of a local variable inside `fun()`. After `fun()` returns, that memory is gone, so reading it is undefined behaviour.
steps: `fun()` makes `int x = 10` on its stack frame and stores `&x` in global `p`.
`fun()` prints 10 and returns - its frame is freed.
`main` reads `*p`, which now points to dead memory.
files.output_note: `Fun -> 10` is correct. `Main -> 0` shows garbage: the old stack slot was reused. On another machine it may show 10 or crash.
files.watch_out: Never return or keep the address of a local variable. Use `new` (see the next file).

check.a: `x` was a local variable; its memory was released when `fun` returned, so the value is no longer guaranteed.

files.title: Pointer to heap memory survives the function
files.what: Same setup as the stack version, but `x` is created with `new`, so the value is still valid in `main`.
steps: `fun()` does `int *x = new int; *x = 10; p = x;`.
Heap memory is not freed when `fun` returns.
`main` safely prints `*p`.

check.q: When is this heap int freed?
check.a: Only when someone calls `delete p;` (the program never does, so the OS frees it at exit).

files.title: Static local variable (empty file)
files.what: The file in the repo is empty (0 bytes); from its name it was meant to show that a `static` local variable also survives after its function returns. The test driver writes that idea as a tiny C program.
steps: A `static int x` inside `fun()` is created once and kept for the whole program run.
`p = &x` is therefore safe to use later in `main`.
Unlike heap memory it needs no `delete`, but there is only one copy shared by all calls.
files.output_note: The driver prints `Fun -> 10` and `Main -> 10`: the static variable is still alive in `main`.
files.watch_out: The source file is empty, so on its own it cannot become a program; the code under the test driver is only an illustration.

check.q: How is a `static` local different from a normal local?
check.a: It is created once and lives until the program ends, instead of dying when the function returns.

files.title: Returning an array from a function
files.what: A function can't safely return a local array, but it can return a pointer to an array made with `new`.
steps: The commented-out `static_array()` shows the wrong way (returning a stack array).
`dynamic_array()` does `new int[5]`, reads 5 values into it and returns `p`.
`main` stores the pointer in `y`, prints the values and calls `delete[] y`.
files.output_note: A blank first line (from the early `cout << endl`) then `5 10 15 20 25 `.

check.q: Why is returning `a` from `int a[5]` inside a function wrong?
check.a: The array lives on that function's stack frame, which is destroyed on return, leaving a dangling pointer.

files.title: Growing an array by copying
files.what: Arrays can't grow in place, so you make a bigger one, copy the old values, and add new ones. Shown for both stack and heap arrays.
steps: Read 3 values into `a[3]`, copy them into `b[5]`, set `b[3]=40`, `b[4]=50`.
Do the same with heap arrays: `p = new int[3]`, `q = new int[5]`.
Copy `p` into `q`, add 40 and 50, print `q`.
`delete[] p` frees the old heap array.
files.input_note: Line 1: three numbers for the static array. Line 2: three numbers for the dynamic array.
files.output_note: The static part prints `10 20 30 40 50`; the dynamic part prints `1 2 3 40 50`. The prompts appear next to the results because all input is fed at once.
files.watch_out: `q` is never deleted; add `delete[] q;` before `return 0;`.

check.q: Why is the heap version better for resizing?
check.a: You can free the old array with `delete[]` and keep only the new one; a stack array stays until its scope ends.

practice_links.name: M. Capital or Small or Digit

recap: Stack variables die with their function; heap variables live until `delete`.
Return heap arrays (pointers) from functions, never local arrays.
An array can't grow: allocate bigger, copy, free the old one.
Watch `int` overflow on products - use `long long`.

check_yourself.q: What is wrong with `int* f(){ int a[3]; return a; }`?
check_yourself.a: `a` is a local stack array; its memory is gone after `f` returns, so the pointer dangles.
Heap memory that is never `delete`d even though nothing uses it any more.

check_yourself.q: How do you free memory from `new int[10]`?

body: Picture a sheet of paper on which you must write the marks of a class, and nobody has told you yet how many students there are. You can rule a thousand lines and waste the page, or rule thirty and run out halfway. What you want is to hear the number first and cut the paper to size after that.

You have met this in C. `int a[5];` fixes the size while you are still typing the program, so the size has to be a guess. `malloc` was the way out: read `n` first, then ask for room for exactly `n` numbers. Module 2 is that same idea in C++ clothes, and it also makes plain what C left vague: where the room comes from, and who takes it back.

The memory your program uses is split in two. Ordinary variables live in the **stack**: `int x = 10;` and `int a[5];` are both there. The stack is automatic. Room is taken when the variable is created and handed back the moment the function it lives in ends. You never ask for it and you never get a say.
The other area is the **heap**. Nothing is taken there unless you ask, and nothing is given back unless you say so. `new` is how you ask, `delete` is how you give back:
intro.snippet:
int x = 10;          // a box on the stack, named x
int *p = new int;    // a box on the heap, no name
*p = 100;            // write 100 into that box
cout << *p << endl;  // 100
delete p;            // hand the box back

body: It is worth drawing, because the heap box has no name of its own. The only way back to it is the address kept in `p`, and `p` itself is an ordinary stack variable:
intro.trace:
stack                   heap
------------            ----------------
x = 10
p = 0x1a2b40 ---------> 0x1a2b40:  100
                        this box has no name;
                        p is the only way to it

body: So `p` is `0x1a2b40`, an address, and `*p` is 100, the thing at that address. That part you know already. **What is new is the pair `new` and `delete`.** No size in bytes to work out, no cast to write: `new int` means one int, `new int[n]` means `n` of them, `delete p` gives back one, `delete[] p` gives back an array.

If you never say `delete`, the box is never given back, not even after you have lost the address that led to it. That is a **memory leak**: memory your program still holds but can no longer reach or use. One leaked int costs 4 bytes and nobody notices; a leak inside a loop that runs a million times eats 4 megabytes and keeps going.

The second use of the heap is the one that makes it worth having. A stack variable dies with its function. If a function stores 10 in a local `x` and hands out `&x`, the address survives but the box does not, and reading through it afterwards means reading memory that is no longer yours. It often still prints 10, so the bug hides. Put the value on the heap and the box is simply still there:

The same rule decides how a function hands an array back to `main`. A local `int a[5]` cannot be returned, because it dies with the function; `int *p = new int[5]` can, because it does not. A third use: no array can be made bigger after it exists. What you can do is ask for a bigger one, copy the old values across and carry on with the new one — three values in a 3-box array become those three plus two more in a 5-box array. The copying costs as many steps as the array is long, which is why you grow in jumps and not one element at a time.

The first five programs below are ordinary practice written with `cin` and `cout`. After them come the memory programs: a dynamic variable, a static array beside a dynamic one, the dying-local trap and its fix, returning an array, and growing one by copying.
